home.meta: VEYRS turns vulnerability findings into ranked, owned and verified decisions: CVE, CVSS, EPSS and CISA KEV correlated with your assets, their exposure and their business impact.
home.hero.lead: VEYRS ranks every finding by what it means to your business — evidence of exploitation, exposure and the value of the asset — and carries each decision through ownership, deadlines and verified remediation.
mock.title: Decision queue
mock.caption: A 9.8 on an isolated lab host ranks below a 6.5 on the payment gateway. That is the system working correctly.
home.std.title: Built on the open standards security teams already rely on
home.problem.title: Scanners say what is wrong. VEYRS says what to fix first.
home.problem.p1: Nobody is short of findings. The shortage is in the answer to “of everything wrong across the estate, what should this team fix this week, and what happens if they don’t?”
home.problem.p2: A scanner cannot answer that: it does not know which host faces the internet or which one takes payments. VEYRS combines severity with the probability of exploitation, evidence of exploitation in the wild, the asset’s exposure and its business impact — and ranks the work accordingly.
home.cmp.title: Same scanner output, different decisions
home.cmp.note: Severity is one input. Exposure, exploitation and business impact decide the order.
home.how.title: From raw findings to verified outcomes
home.how.lead: One chain, five steps. Each step produces something a person can act on and an auditor can check.
home.how.v: Assets and the software on them, matched against the CPE dictionary — with an explicit signal when something cannot be matched, because “nothing is vulnerable” and “nothing is matchable” look identical everywhere else.
home.how.e: Internet-facing, internal or isolated. The same flaw is not the same problem in two places, and the ranking reflects it.
home.how.r: CVSS from v2 to v4.0, combined with EPSS probability, CISA KEV, exposure and business impact. EPSS is a forecast; KEV is a sighting.
home.how.a: A ticket with an owner, a due date and an escalation path, synchronised with Jira or ServiceNow.
home.how.s: “Resolved” is a claim. “Verified” is a later scan that no longer sees the finding — and only a machine assigns it.
home.cap.title: One platform, from scanner output to the board report
home.cap.lead: Bring the tools you already run. VEYRS normalises their output, adds the context they lack and turns it into work with an owner.
home.cap.ingest.d: {n} report formats — network, web, container, code, secrets and cloud — each parsed from the tool’s documented schema and deduplicated per scanner.
home.cap.exec.d: Agents on your jump hosts run scanners under a deny-by-default policy: without an enabled tool and an allow-listed target, nothing runs.
home.cap.intel.d: NVD, EPSS, CISA KEV and CWE synchronised on a schedule, so priorities move when the threat landscape does.
home.cap.risk.d: Findings rank by computed risk, not by CVSS alone. Accepting a risk requires an accepting party and an expiry date.
home.cap.sla.d: SLA clocks by severity and exposure, escalation paths and two-way sync with Jira and ServiceNow — advisory by default.
home.cap.report.d: Executive and technical reports in PDF, XLSX, CSV and JSON, with findings mapped to NIST CSF 2.0, CIS Controls and ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002.
home.prin.title: Every number comes with the number that tells you whether to believe it.
home.prin.lead: A finding count means nothing without a rejected-records count. A clean estate means nothing without inventory coverage. Those pairs are not defensive engineering — they are the product.
home.prin.1.d: A scan that completes less than 80% of its work fails, whatever the scanner’s exit code says. Payload size cannot tell a blind scan from a clean one; coverage can.
home.prin.2.d: A fix counts when a later scan confirms it. An external ticket status never closes a security finding on its own.
home.prin.3.d: Accepting a risk needs an accepting party and an expiry date. An acceptance without an expiry is not a decision, and VEYRS will not record one.
home.trust.title: Built to hold your most sensitive data
home.trust.lead: A vulnerability platform is a map of every weakness you have. VEYRS is designed on that assumption.
home.trust.rls.d: PostgreSQL row-level security, forced on every tenant table. Isolation does not depend on a query remembering a filter.
home.trust.audit.d: Changes and sign-ins are recorded, secrets are redacted before they are written, and database triggers keep the audit tables append-only.
home.trust.auth.d: Argon2id passwords, two-factor codes by app, e-mail or Telegram, and sign-in through OIDC single sign-on, LDAP / Active Directory or RADIUS.
home.trust.secrets.d: Third-party credentials are sealed with versioned encryption and planned key rotation — or kept in an external vault.
home.trust.signed.d: Every release ships SHA-256 checksums with an OpenSSH signature, and the installer verifies both before it runs anything.
home.trust.selfhost.d: VEYRS runs on your infrastructure. External AI providers are off by default; nothing leaves unless you allow it.
home.deploy.title: Runs where your data already lives
home.deploy.lead: One signed installer, two ways to run, and a reference topology for high availability.
home.deploy.native.d: A guided installer for Debian and Ubuntu, the Red Hat family and SUSE: systemd, nginx and PostgreSQL, online or offline.
home.deploy.docker.d: The same platform as a hardened container stack, with a bundled or an external PostgreSQL.
home.deploy.ha.d: Two stateless application nodes behind a proxy and a hot-standby database: an application node can fail without anyone noticing.
final.title: Turn your vulnerability backlog into a decision queue.
final.lead: Open the console, or read how VEYRS is installed, secured and operated.
feat.ingest.title: Ingestion
feat.ingest.lead: {n} report formats, each parser written from the tool’s documented schema.
feat.ingest.net.n: Anchored to hosts; deduplication defaults to the legacy key
feat.ingest.web.n: Granularity preserved: ZAP reports one alert with N endpoints, Nuclei one finding per URL
feat.ingest.img.n: The “host” is an image reference: registry/api:2.4.1 is a tag, not a port
feat.ingest.code.n: Requires target_asset: VEYRS never guesses which asset a finding belongs to
feat.ingest.iac.n: The repository or path is the asset, named explicitly
feat.ingest.cloud.n: The cloud account or resource is the asset, named explicitly
feat.dedupe.note: Deduplication is per scanner and configurable, and the live registry is at GET /engagements/dedupe-registry. Changing an algorithm re-keys existing findings, which creates duplicates rather than updates: treat it as a migration, not a setting.
feat.exec.title: Execution: VEYRS runs scanners, not just imports them
feat.exec.p: Agents are single-file runners you place on a jump host. Enrolment grants nothing: an agent stays inert until an operator enables a specific tool and gives it a non-empty target allow-list. An agent enrolled and forgotten cannot scan anything.
feat.exec.r1.b: AgentTool.enabled, off by default. A declared tool is not an authorised tool.
feat.exec.r2.b: An empty allowed_targets list means inert. Checked twice: when the job is queued and against the agent that claims it.
feat.exec.r3.b: A host name target never matches a CIDR rule.
feat.exec.r4.b: Loopback, link-local and multicast addresses (including 169.254.169.254) need an exact literal entry.
feat.exec.r5.b: require_asset_match (on by default) demands that the host exists in the asset register.
feat.exec.r6.b: Below 80% completion or above a 50% error rate the job fails, whatever the exit code.
feat.intel.title: Threat intelligence
feat.intel.nvd: CVE records and CPE applicability. Can create findings.
feat.intel.cwe: Weakness taxonomy used to classify findings.
feat.intel.p: EPSS and KEV never create findings: a probability or an exploitation flag does not change what is affected, so correlating over them would mean hundreds of thousands of inventory queries a night to learn nothing.
feat.risk.title: Risk-based prioritisation
feat.risk.p1: Findings rank by computed risk, not by CVSS. The inputs are severity (CVSS v2, v3.0, v3.1 and v4.0), EPSS probability, presence in CISA KEV, the asset’s exposure and its business impact; risk profiles set how much each one weighs.
feat.risk.p2: risk_accepted requires an expiry and an accepting party. An acceptance with no expiry is not a decision, it is an abandonment — and the platform will not record one.
feat.sla.title: Ticketing and SLA
feat.sla.clock.d: Driven by severity and exposure, with escalation paths and breach reporting. A due date nobody owns is not an SLA.
feat.sla.itsm.d: Jira and ServiceNow, push and pull. Inbound webhooks are HMAC-authenticated and advisory by default: an external system does not close a security finding unless a transition map says it may.
feat.report.title: Reporting and compliance
feat.report.reports.d: Executive summary, technical detail, compliance posture, SLA performance and remediation trend, exported as PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON — every export carries its provenance.
feat.report.compliance.d: Findings map to NIST CSF 2.0, CIS Controls, ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A and ISO/IEC 27002, so posture is derived from evidence rather than asserted in a spreadsheet.
arch.topology.title: Topology
arch.topology.lead: Two interchangeable application nodes, one node that holds all the state, and a hot standby of that state. The standby belongs on a different physical host from the primary: on the same host it covers the loss of the database node, not the loss of the machine.
arch.d.standby.s: Hot standby on another physical host
arch.d.caption: Reference topology. Every name resolves to the proxy, which chooses the application node.
arch.n1.r: Application plus the scheduled jobs (scan runner, intelligence sync, digest)
arch.n2.r: Application. The scheduled-job units are installed but disabled.
arch.n3.r: PostgreSQL and Redis. The only node with state.
arch.n4.r: Hot standby by streaming replication. Promoted by hand, never automatically.
arch.stateless.title: Why the application nodes hold no state
arch.stateless.p1: Because the failure that actually happens is a process dying, not a data centre burning. A cold-standby clone covers the second and not the first: it needs a person to notice and act. Two stateless nodes behind an upstream cover the first automatically — the proxy marks the dead backend and serves from the other, with nobody looking at a phone at 03:40.
arch.stateless.p2: Verified in production, not assumed: with the API killed on one node, 20 of 20 requests were served; with the whole container stopped, 25 of 25 within six seconds.
arch.dns.note: Failover does not happen in DNS. Every name resolves to the reverse proxy, which chooses the backend. No bookmark ever changes and no TTL is ever waited on.
arch.single.title: Scheduled jobs run on exactly one node
arch.single.p: The scan runner and the intelligence sync are enabled on application node 1 and disabled on node 2, with the units and configuration in place so node 2 can take over in one command. Two runners claiming the same jobs is corruption, not redundancy.
arch.fail.title: What each failure costs
arch.f1: The API dies on one node
arch.f3.i: Scheduled jobs pause; the console is unaffected
arch.f3.r: An operator enables the units on node 2
arch.f4.r: Promote the standby (a manual, deliberate step)
arch.f5: Physical host of the database lost
arch.f5.r: Promote the standby if it runs on another host; otherwise restore the off-host logical dump
arch.prot.title: Data protection
arch.p1.c: Loss of the database node — and of its host, when the standby lives elsewhere. Recovery point of a few seconds.
arch.p1.n: Logical damage: it replicates a DROP faithfully.
arch.p2.c: DROP, a bad migration, corruption. Selective restore.
arch.p3.c: Rollback of a whole container, crash-consistent.
arch.p3.n: Loss of the host — unless the datastore lives on another machine.
arch.prot.note: The dump is copied off the database node and its restorability is proven weekly. Not by checking that the archive parses — a dump taken under row-level security is a well-formed archive whose tables are empty — but by restoring it into a scratch database and comparing row counts and policy counts with production.
arch.promo.title: Promotion is manual on purpose
arch.promo.p: Automatic promotion without a fencing mechanism produces two primaries, and two primaries produce divergent security data that cannot be reconciled afterwards. The runbook:
arch.stack.title: Stack
arch.s.api: FastAPI on uvicorn, four worker processes, bound to loopback behind nginx
arch.s.data.v: PostgreSQL 15 or later, with row-level security forced on every tenant table
arch.s.auth.v: Argon2id, JWT with rotating refresh tokens, two-factor codes, OIDC, LDAP and RADIUS
arch.s.secrets.v: Fernet envelope with versioned ciphertext, or an external vault
arch.s.schema.v: veyrs init-db and veyrs sync-schema: idempotent and additive, no Alembic
arch.s.deps.v: {packages} packages, pinned with hashes and guarded by tests
sec.iso.title: Tenant isolation lives in the database
sec.iso.lead: Every tenant table is protected by PostgreSQL row-level security with FORCE enabled. Isolation is not a WHERE clause the application has to remember, so a bug in a query cannot leak data across tenants. The production API also refuses to start with a database role that could bypass it.
sec.iso.note: The practical consequence: a script that reads production without setting the tenant sees zero rows. Empty is the correct, safe answer to an unscoped query — not evidence that the data is gone.
sec.auth.title: Authentication
sec.auth.r1.b: Argon2id with a per-password salt; at least 12 characters
sec.auth.r2.b: A wrong password, an unknown e-mail, a disabled user and a disabled organisation all return the same 401
sec.auth.r3.b: Per source, increasing back-off after five failures; an account is locked only by failures spread over several addresses
sec.auth.r4.b: Refresh tokens rotate on every use; replaying a used one ends that session. Logout, password change and deactivation end every older access token
sec.auth.r5.b: Codes by authenticator app (TOTP), e-mail or Telegram, with single-use recovery codes; optional per user or required per organisation
sec.auth.r6.b: LDAP / Active Directory, RADIUS and OIDC. Platform administrators are never delegated to a directory or to single sign-on
sec.auth.r7.b: No local password to brute-force — that is the point
sec.mfa.title: Two-factor is a control, not a checkbox
sec.mfa.p: Enrolment takes three steps — enroll, then activate with a working code, and only then is the factor enforced — because enabling it in one step is how administrators lock themselves out of the console they administer. Turning it off requires the password and a code, so a stolen access token cannot strip the second factor from the account it was stolen from.
sec.secrets.title: Secrets
sec.secrets.p1: Third-party credentials (AI providers, ITSM connectors, threat sources, webhook secrets, two-factor seeds) are stored under a Fernet envelope with versioned ciphertext, so keys can be rotated without guessing at the payload — or kept in an external vault. They cannot be hashed: VEYRS has to replay them. In production the application refuses to start without an explicit encryption key.
sec.secrets.p2: The audit log redacts passwords, key hashes and two-factor secrets when it records them, not when it displays them. A redaction applied on the way out is a redaction someone will forget to apply to the next view.
sec.input.title: Untrusted input
sec.input.p: Every scanner report is attacker-influenced data: anyone who can get a finding into a scan can get a string into VEYRS.
sec.input.1: XML entity declarations are refused by the parser (Nessus, Qualys, Greenbone). XXE against a vulnerability platform would be a very good trade for an attacker.
sec.input.2: Metric labels are escaped by the emitter, never by callers. Unmatched routes contribute a constant, and series are capped with an overflow bucket.
sec.input.3: Uploads are size-bounded and land in a scoped engagement; an import that names no engagement is still scoped, never global.
sec.agent.title: The agent authorisation model
sec.agent.p: Agents execute scanners, which makes them the most dangerous component of the product. They are deliberately the least trusted.
sec.agent.1: An agent authenticates with X-Agent-Token and is not a user: it reaches /agents/self/* and nothing else.
sec.agent.2: Two independent switches must both be on before anything runs: the tool is enabled, and the target allow-list is not empty.
sec.agent.3: Targets are authorised twice: when the job is queued and again against the policy of the agent that claims it.
sec.agent.4: Inventory collection is held to the same target policy as scanning. An agent that could rewrite any asset’s software could make a host look clean without running a scanner at all.
sec.obs.title: Observability endpoints
sec.obs.p: /metrics requires a bearer token and answers 404, not 401, when the token is wrong or absent: a probe learns nothing. An address allow-list does not work here, because every request arrives from the reverse proxy — any address-based rule matches the proxy, not the caller.
sec.supply.title: Supply chain
sec.supply.p1: Dependencies are declared, pinned and locked with SHA-256 hashes, and every installer uses --require-hashes: {packages} packages today. The source ships a CycloneDX SBOM generator and an advisory check against OSV.
sec.supply.p2: Parsers were written from each tool’s documented schema. No code was copied from DefectDojo (BSD-3) or Faraday (GPL-3.0).
dl.get.title: Get the release
dl.get.lead: Every release is published on GitHub and signed. Check the signature first, then every file against it, and only then run anything as root.
dl.get.check: --check runs the same requirement checks described below and changes nothing, so run it on the target host before you size anything by hand.
dl.a.setup: The guided installer: native or Docker, online or offline
dl.a.sums: The SHA-256 of every asset and its OpenSSH signature (principal release@veyrs, namespace veyrs-release)
dl.a.src: The release tree; the installer downloads it itself unless you pass --source
dl.a.wheels: The Python packages for a native installation without access to PyPI
dl.get.all: All assets of the latest release
dl.perm.title: Permissions the installation needs
dl.perm.note: The installer must run as root (sudo) and refuses to start otherwise: it installs distribution packages, writes systemd units and, in Docker mode, installs Docker itself. There is no reduced-privilege mode. Every step that needs more than the installation directory is listed here, with the flag that skips it when your site policy reserves that step for someone else.
dl.n2.w: CREATE ROLE, CREATE DATABASE; one scoped pg_hba.conf block only if a password login actually fails (SUSE and the Red Hat family default to ident)
dl.n4.p: Write access to the installation root
dl.n5.p: The owner of the database, not a superuser
dl.n5.w: init-db: tables, row-level security policies, built-in roles
dl.n6.w: Writes /etc/systemd/system/veyrs-api.service and the service account it runs as
dl.n7.w: Writes the console directory and the virtual host, reloads nginx
dl.perm.super: The superuser is needed only to create the role and the databases. The application’s own role is deliberately unprivileged — NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS — and owns its database and nothing else. An external PostgreSQL whose role is a superuser or has BYPASSRLS is refused, because either one switches tenant isolation off.
dl.d1: Installs Docker Engine and the Compose plugin from Docker’s repository when missing, and writes /opt/veyrs-docker (environment file 0600), /usr/local/sbin/veyrs-docker and /etc/veyrs-setup.conf
dl.d2.runs: root, or a member of the docker group
dl.d2: Membership of docker is equivalent to root on that host: grant it as you would grant root
dl.d4: nginx on container port 8080, same hardening
dl.d5: Only CHOWN DAC_OVERRIDE FOWNER SETUID SETGID; it chowns the data volume, then drops to uid 10001 before it touches the database
dl.d6: No NET_RAW: no SYN scanning unless you grant it deliberately
dl.perm.lxc: Docker inside an LXC container needs nesting=1, plus keyctl=1 when the container is unprivileged. Without them the daemon installs but never answers, and the installer stops and says so.
dl.perm.unasked: What the installer will not do unasked
dl.u1: Open the firewall. With firewalld or ufw active it warns and continues; --open-firewall is opt-in.
dl.u2: Overwrite an existing .env, nginx virtual host, database role password or administrator password. A re-run leaves all four alone.
dl.u3: Pass the administrator password on the command line. It is handed over through the environment, never in an argument another user could read with ps.
dl.selinux: SELinux: where it is Enforcing, the installer sets httpd_can_network_connect (without it nginx answers 502 on /api/) and restores the labels on the console directory.
dl.service: The API service does not run as root. The native veyrs-api service runs as the unprivileged veyrs account inside a systemd sandbox — ProtectSystem=strict with /opt/veyrs/var as the only writable path, NoNewPrivileges, PrivateTmp, ProtectHome, MemoryDenyWriteExecute, no capabilities — and the API listens on loopback only.
dl.net.title: Network
dl.net.p: The complete list, with the setting that moves or disables each destination and what to do without it, is in the console under Configure → Platform → Network access.
dl.net.in: 80, or 443 where TLS terminates on the host (native); VEYRS_HTTP_BIND, by default 127.0.0.1:8080 (Docker)
dl.net.loop: The API; nginx proxies it and it is never exposed
dl.net.db: To the database and the cache — localhost unless you split them
dl.net.rhel: native installations on the Red Hat family
dl.net.install: During installation or an update only; the offline paths (the release’s package bundle for native installs, an image bundle for Docker) need none of them
dl.net.intel: At runtime, recommended: vulnerability intelligence. Without it VEYRS keeps running on stale data; NVD, EPSS and KEV files can also be uploaded by hand
dl.net.update: At runtime, optional: the update check and the updater’s download (native installations). VEYRS_UPDATE_URL= switches the check off
dl.net.mfa: Only if two-factor codes by Telegram or e-mail are configured
dl.net.ai: Only if an external AI provider is enabled and allowed (off by default)
dl.hw.title: Hardware: CPU, memory and disk
dl.hw.gates.p: These are the gates of veyrs-setup.sh --check. They decide whether the installation starts; they are not a size for a system that pulls vulnerability intelligence.
dl.g.cpu: The API runs four worker processes; building images is the heaviest moment
dl.g.ram: The running stack fits in 2 GB; building images needs the 4
dl.g.disk.n: On / because that is Docker’s default data root
dl.hw.disk: Disk is driven by threat intelligence, not by your findings. On the reference deployment the database is 5.3 GB with 1,615 findings: about 5.2 GB of it is the NVD corpus, the CPE dictionary and EPSS scores. EPSS history keeps one row per CVE per scored day — about 370,000 rows, roughly 80 MB a day — for VEYRS_EPSS_HISTORY_DAYS days (default 365, about 30 GB; 90 days is about 7 GB). The 5 GB and 12 GB gates above therefore only hold for an installation that never turns the intelligence feeds on.
dl.s1.n: Images, a small database, the optional 84 MB scanner template corpus
dl.s2: Single node with intelligence (native or Docker)
dl.s2.disk: 60 GB (30 GB with 90 days of EPSS history)
dl.s2.n: About 6 GB of database on day one, growing about 80 MB a day until the EPSS retention is reached; WAL; local backups (about 0.9 GB each, growing with it)
dl.s3.n: Stateless; two of them behind a proxy for failover
dl.s4: Split deployment — database node (and its standby)
dl.s4.n: A streaming standby’s replication slot can hold WAL up to max_slot_wal_keep_size while the standby is down — budget for it
dl.hw.follow: CPU and memory follow the number of findings; disk follows the intelligence feeds.
dl.f2: A separate database host is recommended
dl.hw.ref: What the reference deployment actually uses
dl.hw.ref.p: Measured on 2026-10-26 on the split deployment VEYRS itself runs on (two application nodes, one database node with a hot standby), with the intelligence feeds on.
dl.r1.u: 0.9 GB RAM (the API with four workers, about 750 MB) · 6.3 GB disk, operating system and scanner templates included
dl.r2.u: 1.6 GB RAM plus page cache · 18 GB disk: 7.9 GB of PostgreSQL data (2.7 GB of it WAL), the rest backups and the operating system
